newsitem.title: USA: U.S. relaxes ban on Mexican avocados in 19 states.
newsitem.headline: U.S. relaxes ban on Mexican avocados in 19 states.

text.p: The U.S. government announced on Friday it was significantly relaxing a controversial 83-year-old ban on importation of Mexican avocados into the United States.

After two years of emotional debate and exhaustive analysis, the Agriculture Department decided avocados from one Mexican region that met all U.S. import requirements could be shipped into 19 northeastern and midwestern states from November through February, beginning in November this year.

Mexican-grown avocados were banned in 1914 to eliminate the threat of Mexican pests -- especially the fruit fly -- being shipped in with the fruit and damaging U.S. produce and threatening public health. The ban has been eased only once this century to allow the fruit into Alaska.
In its decision to lift the ban, the Agriculture Department said the threat to the American public and U.S. crops was no longer valid.

"After careful scientific analysis and extensive review ... we have determined that if the imported Mexican avocados meet all of our safeguards they will not pose a significant risk of introducing an exotic plant pest into the United States," said Alfred Elder of the Agriculture Department's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service.

States that will be able to import the fruit are Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, West Virginia and Wisconsin.

The Agriculture Department said it would allow avocados to be imported only from approved orchards in the Mexican state of Michoacan. The agency will implement a so-called "systems approach" to closely monitor the imports to prevent any possibility of pests coming into the United States.

The prospects of the ban being lifted, first proposed by the Agriculture Department in July 1995, provoked a huge storm of protest from U.S. avocado growers, with the powerful California Avocado Commission leading the battle.

California grows more than 90 percent of the 300 million lbs (136 million kg) of avocados eaten by Americans every year, and U.S. producers have had a virtual hold on the $1 billion domestic market. The United States currently imports only a small amount of avocados from Chile, Israel and the Dominican Republic.

Analysts estimated at least 30 million lbs (13.6 million kg) of avocados from Mexico would eventually end up in U.S. grocery stores, and the price of U.S.-grown avocados could drop by more than 10 percent.
In recent years, the ban has become a bitter source of contention between the United States and Mexico.

Mexico charged the ban violated world trading laws and threatened to restrict imports of big-ticket U.S. farm products if the ban was not at least partially removed. The normally cohesive U.S. agricultural community was split over the issue, with producers of corn, wheat and other food items that Mexico buys in favor of removing the restrictions.

U.S. trade officials argued that Washington would be hypocritical if it did not relax the ban, since the Clinton administration was pushing other nations to open markets and lift restrictions that were not scientifically based.
